description_full: Domino's Pizza, Inc. operates as a pizza company worldwide. The company operates through three segments: U.S. Stores, International Franchise, and Supply Chain. It offers pizzas under the Domino's brand name through company-owned and franchised stores. The company also provides bread products, wings, boneless chicken, pastas, oven-baked sandwiches, soft drink products and desserts. In addition, it offers parmesan stuffed crust pizza; spicy chicken bacon ranch specialty pizza; and garlic, and cinnamon bread bites, as well as croissant, chocolate volcano, and chicken burst pizzas. Domino's Pizza, Inc. was founded in 1960 and is based in Ann Arbor, Michigan.

CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: Domino's Pizza Inc is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $11.2B market cap on $4.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 98% against a 7% cost of capital — a 90-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 35%.

The business throws off $672M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.5× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 4.9×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 12pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.43x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-8.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 26% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 23% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.81, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $235.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 23% in the 2020 crash, 45% in the 2022 bear market and 81% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 26% below its DCF fair value of $461, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 44%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $268 to $777 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 15.2 vs 10.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 17% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 27 covering analysts target $356 on average, 4% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 98% clears the cost of capital of 7.3% by 90pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.13).
It runs a 35% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.32x.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.5x net debt to EBITDA ($125.7M of cash against $4.8B of debt), with interest covered 4.9x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.3% over 3 years, 3.7% over 5 years and 8.3% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 5.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 17%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 2.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (13 sales, net $11.1M sold).
It returns 5.3% a year to shareholders (3.2% in buybacks and 2.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 17.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 6,200 employees, each generates about $797K of revenue, 2.1x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 8.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $108K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
